items.title: The Voyage of the Beagle and Darwin's Observations

source_refs.note: Darwin's observations on the voyage (PDF 216-217); Figure 24.3 is replaced by an original diagram.

blocks.text: During the voyage Darwin visited tropical rainforests and other new habitats with a great diversity of plants and animals he had never seen. He found rocks containing fossils, suggesting that continents and oceans had changed greatly over time and continue to change, and he dug up fossils of gigantic extinct mammals, showing that organisms looked very different in the past and that living things change over time.

On the Galapagos Islands, a group of 16 small islands, he saw that plants and animals differed from island to island: giant tortoises on one island had saddle-shaped shells and on another dome-shaped shells. Many plants and animals resembled those of South America more than those of other islands, and different species of finch had different beaks, adapted to feeding on completely different foods on different islands.

blocks.alt: Four simple finch heads with different beaks: a large ground finch with a heavy, deep beak for cracking big seeds; a small ground finch with a short beak for small seeds; a cactus finch with a long, pointed beak for probing cactus flowers; and a warbler finch with a thin beak for picking up insects.
blocks.caption: Galapagos finches and their beaks (original diagram after Figure 24.3).
blocks.long_description: On the Galapagos Islands Darwin found that different species of finch on different islands had beaks of different sizes and shapes, and that these were adaptations for feeding on different kinds of food. He reasoned that a new species could arise from an ancestral form as a separated population gradually accumulated adaptations to a different environment, until over many generations the populations became different enough to be separate species.

blocks.text: Darwin sought to explain how the finch species were distributed among the islands. He concluded that the origin of new species and adaptation are closely linked: a new species would arise from an ancestral form by the gradual accumulation of adaptations to a different environment after separation from the original habitat, until over many generations the two populations were different enough to be called separate species.
